name: Lung Abscess

possible: Klebsiella pneumoniae (necrotizing pneumonia, especially in diabetics/alcoholics)
pathogens.why: Lung abscess is most often a polymicrobial anaerobic process following aspiration, with the same oropharyngeal flora implicated in aspiration pneumonia but with a more indolent, necrotizing course requiring longer treatment.

investigations.why: CT better characterizes cavity size, wall thickness, and surrounding parenchymal involvement, and helps distinguish abscess from other cavitary lesions (e.g., malignancy, TB).

investigations.test: Sputum culture (including anaerobic culture if obtainable)
investigations.why: May identify causative organisms, though anaerobic cultures are technically difficult to obtain without invasive sampling.
May identify the organism if bacteremic spread has occurred.

reason: Prolonged fever with cough and foul-smelling sputum, particularly in a patient with aspiration risk, is consistent with lung abscess — a necrotizing pulmonary infection requiring prolonged anaerobic-active antibiotic therapy and imaging to define extent and guide drainage decisions if needed.

clinicalPearls: Roughly 80% of lung abscesses are primary, arising from aspiration in the absence of an underlying pulmonary or systemic disease; the remaining ~20% are secondary to a predisposing process such as bronchial obstruction or immunocompromise (p.1034).

A foul-smelling (putrid) breath, sputum, or empyema is considered essentially diagnostic of an anaerobic lung abscess; abscesses with no isolated pathogen (about 40%) are termed nonspecific and anaerobes are presumed (p.1035).

Primary abscesses favor the dependent segments (posterior segments of upper lobes, superior segments of lower lobes), and the right lung is involved more often than the left because the right mainstem bronchus is less angulated (p.1035).

Anaerobic abscesses often present indolently with night sweats, fatigue, and anemia, whereas non-anaerobic causes such as S. aureus can produce a fulminant course with high fevers and rapid progression (p.1035-1036).

Edentulous patients are thought very unlikely to develop a lung abscess, since teeth (especially with gingivitis/periodontal disease) provide the nidus for the anaerobic/microaerophilic colonization that seeds the lung (p.1034).

Lemierre's syndrome (oropharyngeal infection, classically Fusobacterium necrophorum, with septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein) is a recognized embolic source of lung abscess (p.1034-1035).
Metronidazole alone is inadequate because it covers anaerobes but not the microaerophilic streptococci that are commonly part of the mixed flora of primary abscesses (p.1036).
harrison.pathophysiology: A lung abscess is necrosis and cavitation of lung parenchyma after microbial infection, typically a single dominant cavity >2 cm. In primary disease, anaerobes and microaerophilic streptococci colonizing the gingival crevices are aspirated into a susceptible host who carries an overwhelming aspirated burden or cannot clear it. An initial pneumonitis (worsened by gastric-acid tissue damage) progresses over about 7-14 days to parenchymal necrosis and cavitation, with anaerobes driving more extensive synergistic tissue destruction in polymicrobial infection. Secondary abscesses follow the predisposing mechanism: post-obstructive (tumor/foreign body) impairment of secretion clearance, or impaired host defense in immunocompromise allowing a broad pathogen range. Abscesses may also arise hematogenously from septic emboli (e.g., tricuspid endocarditis, Lemierre's syndrome).
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary malignancy presenting as a cavitary lesion (p.1035)
Vasculitis / autoimmune disease such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (p.1035)
Septic emboli, e.g., from tricuspid valve endocarditis (p.1035)
Pulmonary manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease or pyoderma gangrenosum (p.1035)
infectionMimics: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (and M. avium, M. kansasii) cavitary disease (p.1034)
Endemic fungi: Coccidioides, Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces (p.1034)
Parasitic causes of cavitation: Entamoeba histolytica, Paragonimus westermani, Strongyloides stercoralis (p.1034)
Nocardia, Aspergillus, Mucorales, Cryptococcus, Rhodococcus equi, Pneumocystis jirovecii in immunocompromised hosts (p.1034)
Empyema / pleural space infection (must be distinguished from a peripheral abscess as it may need urgent drainage) (p.1035)
nonInfectiousMimics: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides (p.1035)
additionalInvestigations: CT chest, which defines cavitation earlier than plain film, can reveal an underlying cause such as malignancy, and helps separate a peripheral abscess from a pleural infection (p.1035)
Molecular methods such as 16S rRNA gene amplification for more specific pathogen identification (p.1035)
Serologic studies for opportunistic pathogens (viral/fungal) when abscess is secondary or empirical therapy fails (p.1035)
Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage or protected brush specimen (early if bronchial obstruction is suspected) (p.1035-1036)
Induced sputum for tuberculosis in patients from TB-endemic areas or with TB risk factors such as HIV (p.1036)
Bronchoscopy with biopsy in patients with malignancy risk or atypical presentation (p.1036)
redFlags: Massive aspiration of abscess contents into the airway (p.1036)
Extension to the pleural space with empyema, which may require urgent drainage (p.1035-1036)
Failure to defervesce or radiographic progression despite appropriate therapy (10-20% of patients do not respond) (p.1036)
Abscess >6-8 cm in diameter, which is less likely to respond to antibiotics alone (p.1036)
harrison.prognosis: Mortality for primary lung abscess can be as low as ~2%, but secondary abscesses carry a much higher mortality, reported as high as 75% in some series. Adverse prognostic factors include age >60, malignancy-associated abscess, presence of aerobic bacteria, sepsis at presentation, symptom duration >8 weeks, and abscess size >6 cm. Defervescence on appropriate therapy can take up to 7 days, and 10-20% of patients fail to respond. Larger cavities at presentation predispose to persistent pneumatoceles or bronchiectasis. Prevention centers on airway protection, oral hygiene, minimizing sedation, head-of-bed elevation in aspiration-prone patients, and pathogen prophylaxis in selected immunocompromised hosts (p.1036).
pitfalls: Failure to exclude an obstructing malignancy: in older patients, those with malignancy risk factors, or those lacking clear aspiration risk, early bronchoscopy/biopsy and CT are indicated rather than assuming a primary anaerobic abscess (p.1035-1036).
Treating a presumed primary abscess that does not improve without re-evaluating for a secondary cause (obstruction, unusual pathogen) (p.1036).
Sputum culture may miss the diagnosis: infection is usually polymicrobial and routine cultures often fail to reflect anaerobes (p.1035).
Using metronidazole as monotherapy, which misses microaerophilic streptococci (p.1036).
Misclassifying a peripheral abscess as a pleural infection (empyema) or vice versa, since empyema may need urgent drainage (p.1035).
Underestimating risk in immunocompromised hosts, who are fragile, infected by a wide pathogen range, and warrant early culture-directed diagnostics (p.1035).
harrison.severityClassification: Lung abscesses are classified as primary (~80%, aspiration-related, anaerobe-predominant, no underlying lung/systemic disease) versus secondary (underlying obstruction, systemic illness, or immunocompromise); and by chronicity as acute (<4-6 weeks) versus chronic (~40% of cases). Size >6-8 cm marks lesions less responsive to antibiotics alone (p.1034, p.1036).
